newsitem.title: USA: Dollar falls off perch vs mark, yen by U.S. close.
newsitem.headline: Dollar falls off perch vs mark, yen by U.S. close.

text.p: The dollar fell from its highest level in nearly three years against the mark Tuesday as the German currency was bolstered by a precipitous fall in both the Italian lira and British pound, dealers said.

Mounting fears Italy will not be a member of the first group of European nations forming a single currency and also fading expectations for a Bank of England interest rate rise caused the currencies of those nations to drop sharply.
Dealers bought marks in order to sell lira and sterling, thus strengthening the mark versus the dollar.

"We're seeing strong, significant purchases of marks against periphery countries in Europe such as Italy and Spain and also against sterling," said John Nelson, foreign exchange trading manager at ABN-AMRO Bank.
Against the Japanese yen, an overseas dollar rally peaked just short of Friday's four-year high before faltering in U.S. trade.

Traders speculated that Japanese authorities are prepared to intervene in the currency market in order to keep the dollar trading below the critical level of 125 yen. This sentiment capped the dollar's gains, dealers said.

The dollar's recent strength in overseas trade was aided by mounting fears over the health of China's paramount leader, 92-year-old Deng Xiaoping, which provoked dollar buying as a safe-haven for investors.
China played down fears over the health of Xiaoping which were raised after Communist Party Chief Jiang Zemin cut short an out-of-town trip to visit the ailing patriarch.

"The dollar rallied late in European trade on Monday and remained high. Only a minor extension of this dollar rally was made when the Xiaoping news hit," said Marc Chandler, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
The dollar fell to 123.82/90 yen from 124.08/18 at Tuesday's U.S. open. It hit a high of 124.71 yen overseas, a touch below its recent 124.82 peak.

After reaching a new high of 1.7050 marks, the dollar fell to 1.6850/60 marks by the end of U.S. trade from 1.6985/95. The U.S. unit also retreated from a three-year high against the Swiss franc, closing down at 1.4700/10 from 1.4775/85. Sterling ended barely changed at $1.6060/70 from $1.6062/72.
The lira was hurt by comments from Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi and reported newspaper remarks from Belgian central bank chief Alfonse Verplaetse.

Prodi said on Monday that Germany was less committed to European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) than Italy, fueling rumors Bonn was conspiring to keep the lira out of the first wave of nations joining in the currency's launch.

Verplaetse denied a report in Belgium's De Financieel Economische Tijd, which quoted him as saying EMU should start without Italy since Rome would flunk mandatory criteria for membership which limit the size of national budget deficits.
After Prodi's outspoken allegation, Germany's Juergen Stark, state secretary in the finance ministry, said he knew of no plans aimed at trying to exclude Italy.

Sterling weakened after Bank of England Governor Eddie George said on Monday that a spate of British economic data, along with sterling's recent strength, had diminished the need for an imminent interest rate rise.
The Spanish peseta also fell amid dealer reports of Bank of Spain intervention.
In other trading, the dollar rose to Canadian $1.3545/50 from C$1.3562/67. The Australian dollar fell to $0.7641/46 from $0.7647/57.
